newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa said confident Zaire talks on track.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa said confident Zaire talks on track.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela said through a spokesman on Thursday that President Mobutu Sese Seko of Zaire and rebel leader Laurent Kabila would meet face to face on Friday for the first time, aboard a South African naval vessel off West Africa.
"Tomorrow the two groups will meet on the ship. The discussions will take place tomorrow," Mandela's spokesman Parks Mankahlana told Reuters in Cape Town.

He said Mandela would escort Mobutu to the ship from Pointe Noire, on the coast of Congo, and South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki would accompany Kabila to the vessel from Luanda, the Angolan capital.
Minutes later, the rebel alliance's shadow foreign minister, Bizima Karaha, said from the rebel stronghold of Lubumbashi that the talks had been put off until Sunday.
"President Kabila can only attend on Sunday. That is the time we have for the talks," he said.
A spokesman for Mbeki, Mandela's chief negotiator in the Zaire peace initiative, said however that Karaha could have missed the latest developments.
"The deputy president is leaving now for Angola. He checked and triple-checked half an hour ago and the process is definitely on track.
"We are absolutely confident that the talks will take place on the ship tomorrow," he said.

Analysts said it was possible the rebels were trying to score a point over Mobutu, who had previously postponed the meeting from Friday to Saturday, without knowing that Mobutu had been persuaded to keep to the original schedule.

Officials said earlier on Thursday that Kabila was on his way to Luanda for talks with the Angolan government and would visit other countries in the region before his first direct encounter with Mobutu, then scheduled for Saturday.
U.S. diplomat Bill Richardson also arrived in Luanda on Thursday afternoon.
The summit was first scheduled for Friday aboard the South African navy icebreaker Outeniqua, which has been steaming off the African west coast for several days.
After initially agreeing to a meeting in international waters off the African coast, Mobutu briefly reneged, saying the arrangement was unacceptable.
Richardson persuaded Mobutu earlier this week to keep his appointment with Kabila to discuss a transition to democracy after 32 years of dictatorship.
Some South African analysts have criticised Richardson's late intervention, accusing him of "diplomatic plagiarism" in the final stages of a delicate peace initiative driven by Mandela and Mbeki.
But Mandela, who has been shepherding Mobutu and Kabila towards a direct meeting since February, said through his spokesman he welcomed any positive intervention.
South Africa, the United Nations and the United States are pressing for an early meeting in a bid to prevent worsening civil war and greater suffering for the region's refugees.
"If there is a victory to be scored, it must be scored by Mobutu and Kabila. If there is a gain to be made, it must be made by the people of Zaire," said one South African official.
Late on Thursday, Mandela was reported to be preparing to return to Pretoria from his Transkei homeland, where he celebrated Labour Day with black workers.
He was expected to leave about 7.30 a.m. (0530 GMT) on Friday for Pointe Noire, where he would be met by Congolese President Pascal Lissouba.
"They will jointly meet with President Mobutu at Point Noire and they will proceed together to the ship.
"Deputy President Thabo Mbeki will leave today for Luanda where he will have a chat with Mr Kabila and they will both proceed to the ship on Friday," said Mankahlana.
